routes.description: Establish a cumulative historical route from early Pauline bodily-resurrection testimony through transmitted Gospel and external witness evidence to an identifiable, structured apostolic community continuous with Catholic Christianity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the early sources warrant bodily rather than merely visionary resurrection belief, the transmission and external evidence remain historically usable, and institutional and doctrinal continuities identify a durable apostolic church despite later disputes.

motionBridge.description: Connect convergent resurrection evidence and early ecclesial continuity into a historically credible account of bodily resurrection and Catholic continuity.

centralBridges.description: Show that the earliest Pauline material describes a transformed bodily resurrection and appearances rather than an exclusively internal vision.
Show that Pauline, Gospel, patristic, and hostile-source lines can be historically combined without depending on a single late tradition.
Trace recognizable offices and a substantially stable doctrinal core through early disputes into the ancient apostolic churches.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use shared councils, fathers, and core doctrines across Roman, Eastern, and Syriac churches as support for a common inheritance.
Distinguish continuity-preserving reform and schism from later developments alleged to constitute substantive doctrinal departure.

routes.description: Establish that the cited sources underdetermine bodily resurrection, that transmission and preservation processes weaken claims of independent corroboration, and that early Christian plurality prevents a secure inference to specifically Catholic continuity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if visionary and inherited-report explanations remain viable, surviving texts and hostile witnesses cannot securely resolve transmission and selection uncertainty, and diverse early communities defeat a determinate linear path to later Catholic identity.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined evidence does not sufficiently distinguish bodily resurrection and Catholic continuity from viable skeptical historical alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Show that Paul's experience and reports about other witnesses do not independently establish encounters with a resurrected body.
Show that compositional delay, unidentified sources, copying uncertainty, and selective preservation limit the evidential force of surviving materials.
Show that competing communities and retrospective definitions of orthodoxy obstruct a simple continuity inference from earliest Christianity to Catholicism.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use differing regional churches and changing historical classifications to test claims of uniform institutional and doctrinal development.
Use pre-Reformation reform and the difficulty of individuating Christian traditions to challenge sharp continuity and departure boundaries.

sections.title: Pauline Evidence for Bodily Resurrection and Appearances
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the earliest cited Christian writings establish a tangible transformed body and bodily encounters, or remain compatible with visionary experience and inherited witness reports.

sections.title: Gospel Sources and Textual Transmission
sections.rationale: The historical force of Gospel material depends on whether the interval before composition, source identification, authorial selection, copying, and possible interpolation permit reliable access to early testimony.

sections.title: Hostile Witnesses and Documentary Preservation
sections.rationale: External descriptions can contribute independent corroboration only insofar as their identification of Christians and their survival are not materially distorted by interpolation or selective preservation.

sections.title: Early Orthodoxy, Diversity, and Ecclesial Structure
sections.rationale: The continuity burden turns on whether early offices and doctrinal convergence identify a persistent apostolic church or whether competing groups, regional variation, and later conciliar definitions make that identity retrospective.

sections.title: Apostolic Continuity, Reform, and Later Christian Divisions
sections.rationale: Comparisons among Catholic, Orthodox, Syriac, Protestant, and medieval reform traditions test which shared doctrines and institutions evidence continuity and where legitimate reform, schism, branching, or departure should be located.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: Paul's early, undisputed letters provide early evidence that he believed Christ underwent a bodily resurrection and appeared to him.
moves.attributionBasis: The opening participant explicitly identifies himself as Catholic and frames the historical case affirmatively before Oppy's response.

response.rationale: This is a constructive opening claim, so it has no earlier opposing target; it directly establishes the proposed Pauline bodily-resurrection premise.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly advances an indispensable central premise using the earliest Pauline material.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is recoverable and carefully limited to early undisputed letters, Paul's belief, and an appearance to Paul.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker acknowledges that the letters lack fleshed-out detail and presents them as sufficient evidence of belief, not exhaustive proof.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Early Pauline authorship and the asserted belief form a coherent inference, though the textual bridge to bodily meaning remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies early undisputed Pauline letters but supplies no specific passage or detailed linguistic warrant for bodily resurrection.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central Pauline bodily-reading bridge and supplies the chronological foundation for that route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The selected span states the affirmative premise without materially developing or evaluating a live opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly distinguishes the early Pauline corpus, concedes limited detail, and says Paul believed bodily resurrection and reported an appearance.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Paul's early letters remain compatible with a visionary experience and do not clearly establish a bodily meeting with someone who had died and returned to life.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker directly rejects the preceding Pauline claim, and the dialogue subsequently identifies this skeptical participant as Graham Oppy.

components.text: Whether the early letters clearly describe a bodily encounter rather than an experience compatible with a vision.

response.rationale: The response directly contests the decisive bodily-meeting inference by arguing that the language is unclear and remains compatible with a visionary experience.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive inference from Paul's report to a bodily encounter, although it does not fully analyze the relevant passages.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast between a vision and a meeting with a formerly dead living person is clear, and the conclusion is limited to underdetermination.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Repeated phrases such as 'not clear' and 'my sense' appropriately calibrate a claim of evidential underdetermination.

charity.alternative: The early letters may use bodily-resurrection language even without narrating a detailed physical meeting.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply must distinguish belief in bodily resurrection from evidence that Paul's own appearance involved two tangible bodies.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Compatibility with a vision coherently defeats a claim that the letters clearly establish a bodily meeting, with only textual detail left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The response identifies the crucial ambiguity but offers no passage-level comparison demonstrating why the visionary reading remains textually viable.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central Pauline-underdetermination bridge by attacking the earliest claimed bodily-appearance evidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response targets the stronger bodily-encounter inference rather than denying that Paul could have believed in resurrection, though the distinction is compressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says the material is unclear, contrasts vision with bodily meeting, and denies that the early letters support a meeting of two bodies.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: First Corinthians 15 contrasts mortal and spiritual bodies while still describing the resurrected body as tangible and transformed rather than immaterial.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker presents a Catholic affirmative reading, references his own Greek analysis, and is addressed elsewhere in the exchange as William.

components.text: Whether First Corinthians 15 supports a tangible transformed body rather than an immaterial or merely visionary appearance.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the underdetermination objection by appealing to Paul's mortal/spiritual-body contrast and expressly defending a tangible physical reading.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly addresses the bodily-versus-immaterial issue, though it asserts rather than fully demonstrates the controlling textual interpretation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is clear, but the relation among 'spiritual,' 'physical,' and 'tangible' is asserted without fully stabilizing those terms.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical statement that there is no other reading exceeds the excerpt's compressed warrant, despite acknowledging an immaterial rival interpretation.

charity.alternative: The spiritual-body language may denote an immaterial body or otherwise fail to establish tangible encounters.
charity.decisiveQualification: A transformed body can remain bodily, but that conclusion requires linguistic and contextual support beyond naming the contrast.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A mortal-versus-spiritual contrast can coherently describe transformation without immateriality, but the tangible-body bridge is only partly defended.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: First Corinthians 15 is specifically identified, yet the excerpt provides little Greek, contextual, or comparative support for the preferred reading.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move squarely advances the indispensable central bridge concerning Paul's understanding of the resurrected body.

representationalCharity.rationale: The speaker accurately identifies the rival immaterial reading and attributes it to advocates, but answers it principally with confidence rather than analysis.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes First Corinthians 15, distinguishes mortal and spiritual bodies, calls the result tangible and physical, and acknowledges an immaterial reading.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Paul's claims about the five hundred and other witnesses are secondhand reports that could have furnished the interpretive framework through which he understood his own experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The skeptical speaker refers to Paul in the third person, challenges evidential transmission, and continues Oppy's previously established position.

components.text: Whether Paul's witness list supplies independent firsthand support for bodily resurrection appearances.
Whether Paul's own experience independently confirms the tangible-body interpretation rather than being filtered through inherited reports.

response.rationale: The move distinguishes Paul's personal observation from inherited witness reports and proposes that those reports shaped his interpretation of his own experience.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts both the independence of the witness list and the evidential interpretation of Paul's personal experience.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes personal observation, secondhand reports, and the possible interpretive influence of those reports.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The phrase 'could equally have influenced him' advances a possibility claim proportionate to the limited evidence offered.

charity.alternative: Paul's inherited witness list may preserve genuine early testimony and need not undermine his own experience.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even genuine early reports are not Paul's firsthand observations and therefore do not independently establish what other witnesses encountered.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between firsthand experience and inherited reports validly limits independence, and interpretive filtering is presented as a possibility.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The witness list and its secondhand character are specifically identified, but the psychological filtering hypothesis remains only lightly supported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central Pauline-underdetermination bridge by limiting both corroboration and independence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply does not dismiss the reports as fabricated; it makes the narrower and stronger point about their secondhand and interpretive status.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names the five hundred and other witnesses, calls those claims secondhand, and explains how prior reports could filter Paul's interpretation.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Known interpolations create unresolved copying uncertainty for Christian texts whose earlier versions and underlying sources are unavailable for comparison.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker advances the skeptical manuscript-transmission argument immediately before Albrecht answers with manuscript and interpolation examples.

components.text: Whether the surviving Pauline text warrants the asserted tangible transformed-body interpretation.

response.rationale: The move raises relevant general copying uncertainty but does not contact the decisive exegetical premise or identify copying evidence affecting First Corinthians 15 itself.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is issue-bearing contrary material about textual reliability, but it does not answer the targeted Pauline bodily-reading component.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between detectable interpolation where versions exist and uncertainty where earlier versions are absent is clearly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move frames the result as unresolved uncertainty about reliability rather than asserting that copying corruption actually occurred.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The absence of comparator versions coherently limits detection of copying changes, though it cannot itself establish that alteration occurred.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Known interpolations provide a relevant basis, but no representative text or specific unavailable source is analyzed in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central transmission-preservation uncertainty bridge, even though its selected reply target is only indirectly engaged.

representationalCharity.rationale: The selected span advances a general transmission concern without developing a specific competing reconstruction to test charitably.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts known interpolations detectable from earlier and later versions with texts lacking early comparators and questions source-copying reliability.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: The roughly two-generation interval before Gospel composition leaves uncertain which sources the authors possessed, what those sources contained, and how reliably material was selected and transmitted.
moves.attributionBasis: The skeptical participant initiates a new question about late Gospel dating and develops it until Albrecht begins defending Luke's historical style.

components.text: Whether Paul's specific bodily-resurrection language establishes a tangible transformed body.

response.rationale: The Gospel-delay objection materially bears on cumulative resurrection evidence but does not answer the earlier Pauline linguistic argument selected as its legal target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies relevant contrary historical material while leaving the decisive Pauline transformed-body component uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The temporal interval, unknown sources, selection process, and resulting reliability question are all clearly distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker appropriately presents unknown sources and selection as questions limiting confidence, not proof of unreliability.

charity.alternative: A later author who regards himself as a historian may still transmit reliable earlier source material.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical intention does not identify the sources, their contents, or the author's selection practices.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The identified gap from elapsed time and unknown source handling coherently limits reliability without inferring automatic falsity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The two-generation interval and source questions are concrete, but no particular Gospel source relationship or transmission example is assessed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central transmission-preservation bridge by identifying compositional and source-selection uncertainty.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move expressly allows the historian characterization while identifying the evidential information it does not supply.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies roughly two generations, unknown sources and contents, and uncertainty about how an author selected information given his commitments.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: Patristic testimony about Gospel sources, together with the earlier Pauline material, permits the Gospel traditions to be used as part of a cumulative early historical case.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly adopts the affirmative Catholic position, invokes church fathers and hostile authors, and is addressed as William at the move's conclusion.

components.text: Whether patristic source testimony resolves the unknown-source, source-content, and authorial-selection uncertainties affecting the Gospels.
Whether the cumulative case resolves the absence of earlier textual comparators and copying uncertainty.

response.rationale: The selected evidence shifts to competing groups and hostile identification markers; it bears on convergence but does not answer the decisive source or copying uncertainties.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move offers adjacent cumulative-case material but leaves both identified transmission demands substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The inventory proposition invokes patristic and Pauline convergence, while the selected excerpt chiefly poses questions about groups and hostile markers.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that rival groups definitely did not derive from Jesus is much stronger than the hostile-marker material shown in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: Competing Christian groups could preserve early claims despite differing from later Catholic markers.
charity.decisiveQualification: Hostile identification of some markers does not by itself establish which group uniquely descends from the historical Jesus.

logicalCoherence.rationale: External identification markers can contribute to convergence, but the inference to exclusive historical derivation and reliable Gospel sourcing is underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt mentions enemies of the faith but supplies neither the claimed testimony nor a defended independence or transmission warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move contacts the central convergence bridge, though the selected evidence weakly connects its several source lines.

representationalCharity.rationale: The question largely excludes rival derivation instead of addressing the strongest possibility of diverse early development from shared origins.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks whether Gnostic or other strands came from Jesus and appeals generally to hostile observers identifying markers, without presenting their contents.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: The first centuries contained numerous competing Christian groups, making preconciliar orthodoxy indeterminate until councils established doctrinal boundaries.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker expressly qualifies his expertise while answering Albrecht's continuity question with the skeptical view consistently associated with Oppy.

components.text: Whether competing early Christian groups undermine the inference from selected patristic and hostile markers to a determinate orthodox continuity.

response.rationale: The reply directly rejects a determinate preconciliar orthodoxy by asserting numerous competing groups and locating fixed doctrinal boundaries in councils.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the continuity inference, although it does not provide concrete examples or fully distinguish social prevalence from doctrinal definition.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is clear and temporally bounded, though 'Orthodox' shifts between recognized status and substantive doctrinal identity.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker qualifies expertise and says 'I would have thought,' but the assertion that nothing was orthodox before councils is broader than the warrant.

charity.alternative: A recognizable proto-orthodox core may have existed before councils formally fixed its boundaries.
charity.decisiveQualification: Formal conciliar definition is not identical to prior nonexistence, even if competing groups make earlier identity less determinate.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Plurality coherently complicates simple continuity, but the inference from later conciliar definition to no earlier orthodoxy is insufficiently qualified.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies on a general assertion of many groups without representative groups, texts, prevalence evidence, or institutional comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central early-plurality bridge and challenges determinate continuity before the councils.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly stresses plurality but compresses the strongest distinction between an existing trajectory and later formal definition.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt acknowledges limited expertise, asserts numerous competing groups for the first centuries, and attributes settled orthodoxy to conciliar work.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: The surviving pre-Nicene record may disproportionately preserve the later winners, while contrary materials may have disappeared or been destroyed, obscuring early theological diversity.
moves.attributionBasis: The skeptical speaker answers the request for competing pre-conciliar theologies and frames the historical record through loss and winner-controlled preservation.

components.text: Whether the surviving patristic record is representative enough to establish convergence rather than reflecting preservation by later winners.

response.rationale: The move directly attacks the representativeness of surviving evidence by proposing loss or destruction of materials from defeated early positions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive representativeness premise, though it supports the selection mechanism mainly through plausibility rather than documentary examples.

precisionFindings.rationale: The hypothesis concerns possible disproportionate survival, lost evidence, and obscured diversity; it does not assert universal destruction.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Phrases such as 'may have,' 'strikes me,' and 'not very plausible' appropriately mark an inferential preservation hypothesis.

charity.alternative: Surviving preconciliar evidence may genuinely reflect a dominant continuous tradition despite later winner-controlled preservation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Later recurring divergence makes complete absence of comparable earlier diversity less plausible, but does not quantify the missing record.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Selective survival is a coherent rival explanation for apparent convergence, with the key prevalence and preservation assumptions left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The analogy to postconciliar heresies supplies a reason, but actual destruction, survival rates, and representative lost traditions are not documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central early-plurality bridge by limiting what surviving evidence can establish about earlier uniformity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move allows that evidence may once have existed and advances a comparative plausibility argument rather than alleging wholesale fabrication.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly invokes winner preservation, possible loss or destruction, and an analogy from recurring postconciliar divergence to likely earlier diversity.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Apparently untampered anti-Christian writings may still be unrepresentative because later Christian manuscript preservation could favor hostile texts whose contents were useful to Christian preservers.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker clarifies that his objection concerns survival rather than textual alteration and extends that explanation through the selection-effect conclusion.

components.text: Whether hostile sources provide representative independent corroboration rather than a Christian-selected sample of surviving pagan writings.

response.rationale: The response shifts the issue from textual tampering to survival selection and directly questions whether useful hostile testimony was preferentially preserved.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the independence and representativeness premise, although the excerpt only begins to articulate the selection mechanism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The selection hypothesis is recoverable, but the fragmentary excerpt leaves its preservation agents, corpus, and precise selection rule underdeveloped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker repeatedly labels the suggestion a possible hypothesis and does not claim that selective survival has been demonstrated.

charity.alternative: Untampered hostile testimony may remain independent evidence even though Christians transmitted its manuscripts.
charity.decisiveQualification: Textual authenticity does not itself establish that the surviving hostile corpus is representative of what once existed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Survival selection is logically distinct from tampering and can limit representativeness, though its causal mechanism is only partly stated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move offers a possible selection effect without examples, comparative survival evidence, or a demonstrated Christian preservation preference.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the central preservation-uncertainty bridge by challenging hostile-source representativeness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move preserves the authenticity point and identifies a distinct selection issue rather than conflating preservation with textual alteration.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly presents a possible selection hypothesis and reframes the question around pagan evidence for widespread preconciliar orthodoxy.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: Christianity need not have been widespread before the councils for its first-century offices and persistent structured form to identify the historical community described by outside observers.
moves.attributionBasis: The response presents Catholic institutional continuity in the first person and then explicitly invites the skeptical interlocutor to assess it.

components.text: Whether hostile-source survival is selectively unrepresentative because later Christian preservers favored useful pagan writings.
Whether early conflict and diversity prevent identifying a persistent structured apostolic community.

response.rationale: The move does not answer selective preservation, but it partially answers the broader plurality challenge by arguing that persistent offices identify a structured community despite conflict.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a secondary continuity component while leaving the primary hostile-source selection mechanism unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The offices-and-persistence proposition is clear, though identifying that structured form as 'very clearly Catholic' leaves Catholic identity insufficiently defined.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move acknowledges conflict and limited spread, but the confident Catholic identification outruns the institutional evidence stated in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: A persistent hierarchy could coexist with multiple structured Christian communities and need not uniquely identify later Catholicism.
charity.decisiveQualification: Continuity of offices supports institutional persistence but requires additional evidence of exclusive lineage and stable doctrine.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Persistent offices can support institutional continuity, but the inference from generic offices to uniquely Catholic identity leaves a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Bishops, priests, and deacons are specifically invoked, but first-century dating and continuous uniquely Catholic succession are asserted rather than demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central apostolic-structure continuity bridge through claimed early offices and historical persistence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The speaker concedes fighting and messiness, yet does not fully confront the strongest possibility of multiple hierarchical continuities.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names bishops, priests, and deacons, dates the hierarchy to the first century, concedes conflict, and claims structured persistence to Nicaea.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Christians initially remained a Jewish sect in Roman classification, while limited knowledge of the diaspora and distinct Syrian churches complicates a simple linear account of Catholic institutional continuity.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker expressly states his limited historical knowledge before offering the Jewish-sect and Syrian-church qualifications characteristic of Oppy's skeptical response.

components.text: Whether early Roman classification and divergent regional churches complicate identifying one linear Catholic institutional community.

response.rationale: The reply directly qualifies the claimed linear identification by noting initial Jewish-sect classification and distinct Syrian Christian development.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the continuity inference, but the speaker's limited knowledge and incomplete Syrian example prevent a fully developed answer.

precisionFindings.rationale: Roman classification is clear, but the connection between that label, diaspora history, Syrian churches, and institutional discontinuity remains incomplete.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker openly qualifies historical knowledge and offers the regional evidence as a complication rather than a conclusive defeat.

charity.alternative: Roman classification as a Jewish sect is compatible with an internally developing Christian hierarchy continuous with later Catholicism.
charity.decisiveQualification: External classification alone does not defeat continuity, while divergent regional churches still require substantive comparison.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Regional and classificatory complexity is relevant to linear continuity, but neither point alone establishes institutional divergence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Roman classification is concrete, while the diaspora and Syrian evidence is fragmentary and expressly limited by the speaker's knowledge.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary divergent-communities bridge by introducing early classification and regional variation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move appropriately presents complications rather than treating Roman labeling as decisive, though the Syrian comparison remains unfinished.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says Romans initially regarded Christians as a Jewish sect, notes later change, and begins invoking distinctive Syrian churches while acknowledging limited knowledge.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: Syriac and Roman churches remained substantially aligned in Trinitarian theology, Christology, and Marian belief despite differences of language and later political division.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker clarifies which Syriac church is meant and argues from joint Christological declarations and shared doctrines using an explicitly Catholic perspective.

components.text: Whether Syrian churches represent substantive theological divergence from Roman Christianity rather than linguistic and political difference.

response.rationale: The reply directly contests the Syrian-divergence component through claimed agreement in Trinitarian theology, Christology, Marian belief, and joint declarations.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive regional-divergence premise with multiple substantive comparison points.

precisionFindings.rationale: The doctrinal comparison is clear, but 'Syriac churches' may cover multiple communions whose degree of agreement is not fully differentiated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Joint declarations support convergence, but assertions that the churches believe the same things are broader than the limited doctrinal examples.

charity.alternative: Syriac and Roman churches may share formulas while retaining significant historical, ecclesial, or Christological differences.
charity.decisiveQualification: Joint declarations and shared doctrines establish substantive convergence without proving complete institutional identity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Shared central doctrines and joint declarations coherently answer a divergence claim, while the inference to broad sameness needs scope limits.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several doctrines and joint Christological declarations are specifically cited, but documents, dates, and relevant Syriac communions are not identified.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly advances the subsidiary cross-church convergence bridge through direct Roman-Syriac doctrinal comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges different language and later division, but understates possible substantive differences beyond the listed doctrines.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites different language, similar Trinitarian theology, joint Christological declarations, and shared beliefs concerning Mary and Christ.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, and Syriac churches share central doctrines and conciliar inheritance, while the papacy remains their principal major institutional division.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker identifies papal authority as the chief Catholic-Orthodox dispute while repeatedly describing Catholic, Orthodox, and Syriac churches as apostolic churches.

components.text: Whether Catholic, Orthodox, and Syriac traditions share enough doctrine and conciliar inheritance to count as a common apostolic family.

response.rationale: The move answers regional-divergence concerns by identifying shared Christology, councils, and a common apostolic category while conceding incomplete uniformity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts substantive commonality and expressly qualifies the claim, though lineage and early institutional transmission remain compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim clearly identifies the compared churches, their shared core, incomplete uniformity, and papal authority as a major division.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker expressly denies complete uniformity and limits the conclusion to substantial commonality among apostolic churches.

charity.alternative: Major papal and conciliar divisions may prevent treating these churches as one continuous institution.
charity.decisiveQualification: Shared councils and core doctrines support common inheritance without erasing real institutional division.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Shared councils and central doctrines validly support common inheritance, with the further bridge to one continuous Catholic institution left bounded.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Christology and seven shared councils provide specific support, though Syriac conciliar variation and papal history are not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It advances the central apostolic-structure continuity bridge by identifying a shared doctrinal and conciliar core.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly concedes nonuniformity and highlights common inheritance rather than claiming that all institutional disputes are trivial.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes shared Christology and seven councils, concedes incomplete uniformity, and groups Catholic, Orthodox, and Syriac bodies as apostolic churches.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: Earlier reform movements retained characteristic Catholic teachings, whereas the Reformation progressively discarded such teachings and became a distinct religious system.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly frames the comparison as the Catholic view and contrasts preserved medieval beliefs with Luther, Calvin, and other Protestant traditions.

components.text: Whether early regional and classificatory divergence complicates a linear account of Catholic institutional continuity.

response.rationale: The move addresses later reform boundaries and is relevant to continuity, but it does not answer the earlier Jewish-sect or Syrian-divergence components.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies issue-bearing material about later continuity while leaving the decisive earlier regional-divergence demand uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The historical contrast is recoverable, but 'reform,' 'shedding,' and 'different religious system' lack explicit criteria for doctrinal departure.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker marks the conclusion as his assessment and notes possible original reform intent, but the system-level conclusion exceeds the examples.

charity.alternative: Reformation traditions may represent reforming Christian branches despite rejecting several medieval Catholic teachings.
charity.decisiveQualification: Loss of listed doctrines shows departure from Catholic teaching but does not alone settle individuation as a separate religious system.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Retention versus rejection of doctrines supports a continuity contrast, but no principled threshold establishes when reform becomes a new system.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Marian teaching, purgatory, and prayer for the dead are concrete examples, but the historical comparison is selective and undocumented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the subsidiary reform-boundaries bridge by contrasting continuity-preserving reform with doctrinal departure.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges Luther's possible reform intent yet treats doctrinal shedding as largely sufficient for a stronger taxonomic conclusion.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt lists Marian beliefs, purgatory, and prayer for the dead, contrasts earlier reform with Reformation shedding, and qualifies Luther's original intention.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: Catholic and Orthodox theology remains substantially compatible despite popular hostility, linguistic differences, and disputes over teachings such as purgatory and the Immaculate Conception.
moves.attributionBasis: The response concedes Orthodox hostility toward Catholics but appeals to Orthodox acceptance of disputed doctrines and Catholic recognition of valid apostolic orders.

components.text: Whether early Jewish classification and Syrian regional difference obstruct a simple Catholic continuity account.

response.rationale: The move supplies relevant later cross-church compatibility evidence but does not address the earlier Roman-classification or Syrian-history complications directly.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It bears on broad continuity through Catholic-Orthodox comparison while leaving the selected earlier divergence demand unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The examples are clear, but phrases such as 'a lot' and 'not too far apart' leave prevalence and the degree of compatibility imprecise.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker acknowledges hostility and linguistic difference, though unspecified Orthodox acceptance weakly supports the breadth of compatibility claimed.

charity.alternative: Orthodox acceptance of particular Catholic formulations may be limited, qualified, or contested within Orthodoxy.
charity.decisiveQualification: Some theological compatibility and mutual recognition do not establish broad consensus or institutional unity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Compatibility on disputed teachings and recognition of apostolic orders support closeness, though they do not resolve all institutional differences.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Purgatory, the Immaculate Conception, and apostolic orders are specific topics, but no representative Orthodox authorities or proportions are supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially advances the subsidiary cross-church convergence bridge through concrete Catholic-Orthodox comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move concedes popular hostility and Latin framing but relies on unspecific claims about how many Orthodox accept disputed doctrines.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt claims some Orthodox accept purgatory and the Immaculate Conception, notes Latin-language differences, and invokes apostolic-church recognition.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Protestant traditions are better classified as branches of Christianity because they share scripture and history with Catholicism, and substantial internal differences do not settle how religions should be individuated.
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy's response develops a comparative taxonomy of Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Buddhism, and Hinduism to explain how shared and distinguishing features classify religions.

components.text: Whether substantial doctrinal differences justify classifying Protestant traditions as a separate religion rather than branches of Christianity.
Whether shared scripture and history can ground a broader Christian family despite major internal institutional differences.

response.rationale: The reply directly contests the taxonomic inference from doctrinal difference, proposing shared scripture and history as grounds for branch classification.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly addresses the classification criterion and explains why substantial perceived differences do not decide religious individuation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition clearly distinguishes branches from separate religions and identifies shared scripture and history as classificatory features.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker advances a comparative classificatory judgment rather than claiming a uniquely necessary taxonomy.

charity.alternative: Catholic-Protestant doctrinal differences may be sufficiently fundamental to warrant separate-religion classification.
charity.decisiveQualification: Magnitude of difference depends on individuation criteria, while shared scripture and history support branch classification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Shared scripture and history coherently support branch classification, and the argument correctly exposes the need for individuation criteria.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The shared features and cross-religion comparisons are relevant, but no systematic taxonomy is defended against rival criteria.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly advances the subsidiary branch-and-reform complexity bridge by challenging a sharp departure boundary.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges that the differences seem enormous to Catholics and answers with an explicit alternative taxonomy rather than minimizing them.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares major religious groupings, identifies scripture and history shared by Catholics and Protestants, and argues for branch classification despite differences.
